title: Start here
text: A small farm, built one working loop at a time. The current plan in one place: build the farm software on the Mac now, then connect and commission the robot in Japan from September 30. Read the software roadmap Assemble the robot step by step Understand the printed kits Now · Mac only Build the software skeleton Device adapters, simulator, evidence store, care-cycle state machine and the exception viewer — all runnable before the robot exists. Next · Japan Commission one care cycle Park the robot. Inspect, measure, make a supervised bottle pour, verify the outcome and recover from interruptions. Later · gated Earn more autonomy Task demonstrations, held-out evaluation, longer observation windows and only then additional care or mobility. Status, September 26: no planter parts have been printed and no growing test has happened. The K1 Max jammed (PLA in the nozzle; the extruder clicks) after the first job was aborted. Printing resumes once the nozzle is cleared or replaced with a 0.4 mm needle/nozzle kit. The earlier “NY pre-trial” is removed from this guide; the first crop will be sown in Japan or in a household tray if the prints are still missing. What we have decided Topic Current direction Status Watering A small robot-held pouring bottle. Human refill. Chosen; grip/spout and accurate pours untested. Growing Rectangular wicking planter and square covered germination kit. Each can finish a crop. Not printed yet; printer jammed. No leak/wick test has been done. Sensing One removable light paddle. Moisture probe and relay deferred for paper trays. Recommended first build; human water/wetness checks before refills. Cameras Use the robot’s head/wrist cameras initially. No separate overhead camera in the first build. Computer The Mac connects to robot interfaces, cameras and ESP32 through the owned powered USB hub. Physical connections still to commission. Battery Anker C300 DC received. Not used in V0; robot runs on its wall supplies while parked. 12 V harness from the car outlet still undesigned and unfused. Furniture Free fully printed modular table for the planters; separate cart for the robot. Table chosen; editable model files still missing. Software Eight-layer farm program on the Mac over LeRobot: adapters, skills, perception, care cycle, evidence, viewer, Jev/Astra shadow, learning loop. Roadmap only; no code written as of Sep 26. Deck . Actual planter meshes; conceptual table/robot placement. Bottle spout is a placeholder. Height, reach and structural capacity are untested. The next three useful actions Answer the six roadmap decisions , then start Phase 0: adapters, simulator, evidence store and viewer on the Mac. Clear the K1 Max nozzle (heat to ~220 °C, 0.4 mm needle from below, or swap the nozzle), then print the two kits. Download the table’s model files. The ZIP received contains Prusa MINI G-code, not the 13 editable 3MF models. Removed from V0: electric watering pump, external reservoir, hoses/float switches, scale hardware, separate overhead camera and leak pads. The requested silicone mat, adhesive rubber sheets, plant labels and measuring syringes remain out. Use household measuring materials. This handbook resolves newer decisions over the original deck/redline. “Selected”, “printed”, “connected” and “validated” mean different things; every unresolved fit is listed where it matters. title: Robot assembly
text: Assemble the robot, one working step at a time. A numbered build guide for the recorded WowRobo two-wheel Combo, Mac, powered hub and farm accessories. Each step names the parts, connections and a completion check. Build the robot first, then add one light tool. For the current paper-grown microgreens, our recommendation is to defer the moisture probe, probe relay and contact holder. Existing cameras plus human water checks support the first supervised trial. This does not yet provide unattended watering. Identify your kit 1–4 · Mechanical 5–8 · Mac and motion 9–11 · Light tool 12–14 · Trays and water 15–16 · Optional parts Connection checklist Tick each checkpoint only after doing it. Checks save in this browser, using the same notebook as the growing trial. This page cannot sense the robot or run it. Use the instructions for the two-wheel kit Your transcript records the WowRobo Combo with assembled SO101 follower arms, two directional drive wheels, two head servos, three cameras, motor boards, robot wiring and two 12V supplies. The current vendor listing calls this XLeRobot 0.4.0. Check the packing list and labels before assembly; the delivered revision has not been inspected here. Watch WowRobo assembly video Two-wheel reference The dedicated two-wheel documentation is still under construction. Use the vendor video for the exact order of brackets, bearings and screws. The older general guide depicts three omni-wheels: its wheel positions, third motor and motor-ID map must not be copied into this build. The steps below organize our integration work; they do not invent missing vendor dimensions or screw lengths. Vendor listing . 1–4 · Build a stable, dry robot Step 01 Lay out and identify the parts On the bench: WowRobo boxes, IKEA cart, hub, Mac; leave the battery disconnected. Group the two arms and their motor controllers, two drive assemblies, head assembly, three cameras, bracket/fastener bags, two motor supplies and supplied USB/motor leads. Keep the original bags with their labels. Photograph motor and adapter labels. Confirm this is the two-wheel servo version and that each motor supply matches its controller and motors. An adapter fitting the socket is not sufficient. Set aside the farm sensors, growing parts and battery. Have a screwdriver/hex keys matching the supplied screws and a borrowed multimeter for electrical checks. Kit revision, voltage labels and all supplied part groups identified. Step 02 Assemble the IKEA cart and drive base On the bench: Cart, two drive modules, printed brackets, bearings, supplied screws and motor extensions. Assemble the cart to its own manual. Before adding the arms, compare the bracket fit with the two-wheel vendor video; do not force a bracket designed for a different cart size. Build and mount each drive module in the video’s orientation and screw order. Use the kit’s bearings, wheel hubs and fasteners; do not substitute the older three-wheel plate. Route supplied motor extensions upward with protected edges and slack. Keep wheels free of dangling leads. Do not cut cart mesh until the delivered bracket and cable route establish where an opening is needed. Base sits securely, wheels clear the structure, and no lead can enter a wheel. Step 03 Mount the arms and head On the bench: Assembled follower arms, top mounts/clamps, head pan/tilt parts, three camera mounts. Support each arm while fastening its mount to the top structure in the vendor orientation. Skip rebuilding an already assembled arm; check for loose joints and cracked prints. Assemble the head pan/tilt mechanism using the supplied hardware. Mount the head camera and each wrist camera if not already fitted. Leave the grippers empty. Place the intended plant surface beside the parked cart and check approximate reach without forcing any joint. The planter table is separate from the robot cart. Both arm bases and the head are secure; cameras have unobstructed views. Step 04 Finish robot cabling before power On the bench: Supplied motor harnesses, camera leads, motor-controller USB cables and cable retainers. Use the delivered wiring map to connect each motor chain to the correct controller, including head and drive extensions. Label the two controller USB leads so they cannot be confused later. Keep motor power disconnected while changing motor plugs. Match connector orientation and pin order; do not splice the farm wire into the motor chain. Retain camera and motor cables at fixed points, with service loops at moving joints. Check that wrist motion cannot pull a plug or stretch a cable. Robot wiring matches the delivered revision and all plugs are seated with power off. For unassembled arms, use the SO101 joint-by-joint instructions . Both XLeRobot arms are followers; a generic leader/follower tutorial does not make one of these a leader. 5–8 · Connect the Mac and prove basic motion USB carries control and camera data. Motor power is separate. Probe equipment shown in the broader render is optional for the paper-tray build. Step 05 Connect the powered hub and identify USB devices On the bench: RSHTECH RSH-ST07, its adapter and upstream cable, MacBook, robot USB leads. Connect the hub’s own supplied power adapter, then its upstream data cable to the Mac’s USB 3-capable port. Keep the Mac on its charger. Do not assume a downstream charging port is the hub’s upstream port. Plug in one motor controller at a time and record its serial-device name, then connect each camera and identify head, left wrist and right wrist by covering the lens briefly. Use the connection checklist below for port labels. Nothing on a USB cable alone powers the arm motors. Two controller identities and three camera identities recorded without guessing indices. Step 06 Install a matching robot software version On the bench: Mac, XLeRobot source and compatible LeRobot environment. Follow the XLeRobot installation guide and its compatible LeRobot revision; record both versions. Do not mix commands from old tutorials with a newly upgraded environment. Use the SO101 guide’s port-discovery tool to map the actual Mac serial ports. Configure those paths in the robot settings instead of Linux /dev/ttyACM names. Select the two-wheel configuration and its expected motor map. Check that the installed code supports the delivered base before commanding it. macOS support for individual serial tools is not proof that every full-robot demo works. Software versions, Mac ports, camera names and two-wheel profile recorded. Step 07 Power, identify and calibrate one arm at a time On the bench: Matched kit motor supply, empty supported arm, reachable power disconnect. Confirm adapter input accepts the local mains and output matches the motor labels. Use the supplied wall supplies for commissioning. Apply motor power last; disconnect it before changing motor wiring. Check the preconfigured motor IDs before changing them. If configuration is required, use the documented one-motor-at-a-time procedure; never rename a whole connected chain blindly. Calibrate each follower arm with a unique name. Follow the tool’s midpoint and range prompts with torque disabled as directed; support the arm and stay within mechanical limits. Save the resulting calibration files. Both arms report the expected motors and have separate saved calibrations. Step 08 Test cameras and small movements without water On the bench: Assembled robot, all USB devices, empty grippers and empty work area. Start a single-joint control example at conservative motion limits. Test direction and stopping on one arm, then the other, then the head. Keep base motion disabled during the first farm setup. Open the camera streams together at modest supported resolution/frame rate. Label the views and check for dropped frames while moving an arm; lower bandwidth if necessary. Test the configured stop action with empty grippers and supported arms. Once controls are dependable, rehearse reaching an empty tray and returning to rest. Small motions, camera coverage and stopping work together without cable pulls or USB resets. References: XLeRobot installation , SO101 port setup/calibration , single-arm examples . These are setup instructions; no robot software has been installed or tested by this website. 9–11 · Add just one light sensor Use one BH1750, with its sensing face upward. The ESP32 stays on the dry robot body. The gripper holds the paddle only while taking a reading. Step 09 Wire a short light-sensor circuit on the bench On the bench: One ELEGOO ESP32, one BH1750, USB data cable, breadboard and jumper wires. With USB unplugged, read the labels on both boards. Fit headers only if needed; solder loose headers into their plated holes. Already installed headers require no soldering. For a verified ESP-WROOM-32 board, our proposed assignment is BH1750 VCC to ESP32 3V3, GND to GND, SDA to GPIO21 and SCL to GPIO22. Match by GPIO label, not physical pin number. Confirm the actual breakout accepts 3.3V and its bus pull-ups do not exceed 3.3V. Check for shorts, then power the ESP32 only through its USB data cable from the hub. Configure firmware to the same SDA/SCL pins, detect the sensor and log lux over serial. Cover/uncover the sensor and confirm the reading changes. Light readings reach the Mac and change reliably when shaded. Step 10 Fit the printed paddle and flexible harness On the bench: Light paddle prototype, BH1750, flexible wire, retained connector and dry ESP32 enclosure. Dry-fit the actual board to the paddle; the prototype is not a guarantee of fit. Secure the board without covering the light-sensitive face or shorting its underside. Replace the short bench jumpers with a retained four-conductor harness. Keep the ESP32 on the cart and the light board on the paddle. The robot’s supplied servo cables are occupied and are not a spare light-sensor bus. Provide strain relief at the paddle and cart, service loops at joints, and a parked tool rest. Test the entire intended reach while logging sensor errors. If the longer I²C link fails, shorten/rework it before trusting readings. Paddle stays secure and the complete moving harness passes a reach test. Step 11 Finish durable connections and repeatable light measurements On the bench: Perfboard/terminals if needed, insulation, fasteners and tool rest. If using perfboard, solder the headers/terminal pins and required interconnects on the dry bench. Check continuity against the tested circuit. Breadboard contacts are temporary, not a moving-arm connector. Insulate exposed splices with suitable sleeves or enclosed connectors; heat-shrink is only needed where there is an exposed joint. Fasten the electronics clear of water and keep the USB connector accessible. Teach a pose at canopy height with the face upward and the robot out of its light path. Stop moving, collect repeated fresh readings and record pose/time. Park the light tool before picking up a bottle. Lux readings do not directly measure plant-useful PPFD. One reproducible light-reading pose and one reliable tool-rest pose established. The GPIO assignment above is a project proposal for the recorded ESP-WROOM-32 board, not a verified photo of the delivered ELEGOO pinout. Espressif reference . The board’s own pin labels and documentation take precedence. 12–14 · Add trays and supervised watering The water under the cress tray is a small built-in supply. The robot-held bottle replenishes it. An external tank and pump are not part of this setup. Step 12 Assemble and test both growing kits by hand On the bench: Cress trough, holder and four insets; square outer tray and insert; paper and water. Follow the combined growing guide for fit, leak and paper-wick tests. Use the square tray’s printed cover when available, or a loose household cover for the trial. Leave an accessible refill opening and inspection spot. Check that paper wets across the seeded area, not just where it first touches water. The square kit needs an actual capillary connection; simply adding water below an elevated insert does not prove self-watering. Start on a stable household surface. Add the modular printed table only after its actual joints, stiffness and reach are checked. Use repeatable tray locations so a taught pour target does not move. Both trays pass hand-operated leak/wetness checks and sit in repeatable positions. Step 13 Teach an empty bottle pickup and return On the bench: Small bottle, suitable outlet, bottle rest, robot gripper and empty tray. Check grip width and retention with an empty bottle. The selected Nalgene container has a wide mouth: validate a fitted spout or use an existing bottle with a controlled outlet. The rendered spout is not a finished printable design. Place the bottle in a repeatable rest outside the crop. Teach pickup, approach to the refill opening, upright recovery and return while empty. Check wrist-camera view, clearance above the tray rim and cable slack through the whole path. A manual spray bottle is for hand use until trigger actuation is proven. Empty bottle can be picked up, aimed and returned without slipping or colliding. Step 14 Try tiny supervised pours and record results On the bench: Small measured water fill, kitchen measuring container, household catch dish and towel. First pour into a kitchen measure over a catch dish, with a person supervising. Record starting fill, pose and actual water delivered. Repeat across different fill levels; tilt duration alone does not establish a dose. After that works, try a small refill of the empty planter. Check for overflow and verify the paper still receives water. Keep the Mac, hub and sensor electronics clear of the wet area. For the initial crop, a person checks water reserve and paper wetness and authorizes each refill. Cameras record evidence; an obscured view is unknown. Do not replace the removed probe with an unvalidated camera-only autonomous watering rule. Supervised pours and upright recovery work; a human remains responsible for watering decisions. Open the combined growing and kit instructions · Why the moisture probe is optional 15–16 · Add only what the next test needs Step 15 Keep optional sensor parts off the first build On the bench: SHT31, moisture probe, relay modules and moisture-holder prototypes. An optional SHT31 measures air temperature/humidity. If wanted, mount it on the dry body in ventilated air, away from motor/electronics heat; it does not need to ride on the arm. Add it to the verified 3.3V-compatible I²C bus only after checking its labels and address. Defer the SparkFun moisture probe and its power relay for the paper-tray build. They are retained in the reference diagrams for a future comparison experiment, not required connections. If later testing the probe, validate repeated contact on sacrificial paper, switched power, dry/damp/wet discrimination and contamination/cleaning before mounting it near a crop. A water-depth solution is a different experiment. Optional parts explicitly marked installed or deferred; absent probe does not become a fake dry reading. Step 16 Commission battery power and mobility separately On the bench: Owned Anker C300 DC, verified conversion cables/adapters, matched robot inputs. Keep using wall power until the motor power path is checked. The transcript mentions two USB-C PD-to-12V cables, but their actual availability and electrical suitability remain unverified. For every powered device, verify negotiated output voltage, polarity, barrel size, continuous/peak current and simultaneous-port behavior. The hub needs its own matched supply path; it cannot be assumed to run from an arbitrary USB-A port. Secure the battery low on the cart. Test power stability with the full load before untethered driving. Use the two-wheel base profile and a clear area for the first drive test; farm care remains parked. Battery conversion and base motion separately verified, or explicitly deferred. Connection checklist: what plugs into what? Part Destination Mount / joining method Hub upstream cable Mac USB 3-capable port Plug-in; hub secured on dry cart. Motor controller A and B USB Two hub data ports Kit USB cables; label A/B. Separate matched motor supplies. Head + two wrist cameras Three hub data ports Supplied mounts and screws; slack at head/wrist joints. One ESP32 USB Sixth hub data port Data-capable cable; dry enclosure on robot body. Seventh port remains spare. One BH1750 ESP32 3V3, GND, SDA and SCL Printed paddle plus retained four-wire harness; headers may need solder. Optional SHT31 Verified compatible ESP32 I²C bus Body-mounted; optional air context. Moisture probe and relay Not connected in recommended first build Deferred with probe holder and probe-specific harness. Bottle and rest Mechanical grip only; no electrical connection Measured grip and outlet; water added by a person. Planters and table No electrical connection Trays stay on a stable surface; robot reaches them. Perfboard / breadboard / wire / fasteners Support the light circuit and cable retention Bench-test first; solder only loose headers, chosen perfboard interconnects or splices. The full robot uses five hub data ports; the light-sensor controller adds one. No added pump, scale, external reservoir, overhead camera or second computer is needed for this supervised configuration. Remaining physical fit checks: delivered kit revision, paddle/board retention, bottle grip/outlet, enclosure/fasteners and moving cable length. These depend on the actual parts; the existing Blender scenes and tool STLs are prototypes, not evidence that those fits have passed.

Open the 16-step robot assembly guide Do these microgreen trays need the soil-moisture probe? No, not for the initial paper-grown trial. We recommend deferring the probe and its relay. Keep one light paddle if you want robotic light measurements. The planters themselves need no electronics. The cress trough stores water below the growing surface. Paper must remain connected to that water. Water in the trough and wetness at the seeds are two separate checks. Question First-build check What the probe would tell us Is there water left below the plants? A person checks the accessible refill area; record a photo when visible. Touching the paper does not measure water depth. Is water reaching the growing surface? Inspect a seed-free edge and check paper wetness by hand with clean hands, without disturbing roots. Repeat at more than one area. Conductivity only at the contact patch, if contact is repeatable. Should the robot refill? A person reviews both checks and authorizes a small tested pour. A reading alone cannot establish the needed dose or rule out wick failure. The SparkFun guide describes a resistive conductivity measurement and recommends powering only for readings to reduce corrosion. On our thin paper, contact pressure, contact area and water chemistry can change the result. That makes it an optional experiment, not a validated requirement. It might become useful with thicker growing media or a demonstrably repeatable paper contact method. For the square kit: do not assume the perforated insert wicks by itself. Establish the paper/mat’s capillary connection by hand before depending on water beneath it. A full lower tray can coexist with a dry growing surface. For future unattended care: removing the probe does not make cameras a proven replacement. Water-level visibility, a validated level sensor/indicator, or another independent measurement could be evaluated later. A hidden waterline or uncertain wetness pauses automatic watering. Optional probe experiment: calibration and contact testing Calibration means recording what your installed probe reads on the actual paper with known dry, damp and wet examples. Repeat placements, save the raw range and define valid/ambiguous readings. Do not invent a universal percentage or label voltage as volumetric soil moisture. Contact testing means proving the probe really touches the intended patch consistently without hitting the plastic or crushing the crop. Include “hovering/not touching” trials: they must be INVALID, not interpreted as dry. A compliant printed holder/depth stop helps; software cannot correct a probe that misses the paper. For light, extend the paddle to canopy height, face upward, avoid shadows, stop moving and collect fresh conversions. Start with roughly ten readings over two seconds at default timing, logging median/spread and pose. Reject stale/saturated/bus-error samples. Repeated readings improve repeatability, not absolute calibration; lux is not PPFD. ROHM datasheet . Power and cameras still need commissioning Start from the robot’s supplied wall adapters; check that the actual labels accept Japan’s 100V mains. The owned 288Wh C300 DC is not an already completed motor-power solution: its connector, voltage/current capacity and protection path must match the robot. Do not assume USB-C alone supplies fixed 12V motor power. A fixed overview camera would need its own mount and cable path back to a computer; a mobile robot cannot remain tethered to a fixed camera indefinitely. Our initial choice avoids that extra camera: use the existing head/wrist views and validate that they cover the watering area. No Raspberry Pi, depth camera, scale or pump purchase is required for the initial setup shown here.

title: Software roadmap
text: Software roadmap The farm program end to end: the hardware it drives, the XLeRobot code it stands on, the seven parts we write, how one care cycle flows through them, and the order to build it. ← 01 / 18 → Outline Present 01 The farm software, end to end Software roadmap · rebuilt Sep 26, 2026 02 The kit is a body with reflexes. The farm needs a routine, a memory and a conscience. Why write anything at all 03 Everything is a USB device on one Mac The physical system 04 XLeRobot’s code base, layer by layer What already exists 05 Eight layers, seven of them ours Architecture 06 Device adapters: one interface, four devices Layer 1 07 Skills: eight motions with contracts Layer 2 08 Perception: six outputs, each with an unknown Layer 3 09 The care cycle: a state machine that would rather stop than guess Layer 4 10 Evidence store: intent, attempt, outcome — in that order Layer 5 11 The exception viewer: the reason, the evidence and the eligible next steps Layer 6a 12 Jev and Astra: advice with no hands Layer 6b 13 The learning loop: skills graduate, recipes change between cohorts Layer 7 14 One cycle, thirteen messages, seven lanes End to end 15 The simulator is the same program with fakes plugged in Building it before the robot exists 16 One profile names what exists; code enforces what may move Config, safety, deferrals 17 Five phases, five gates, Sep 26 → Oct 10 Build order 18 Six decisions, each with a default Your call Software roadmap · rebuilt Sep 26, 2026 · 01 / 18 The farm software, end to end What we are building, what already exists, how the parts connect, and the order to build them in. 1 · Device adapters 2 · Skills 3 · Perception 4 · Care cycle 5 · Evidence 6 · Review 7 · Learning What the deck covers The hardware we own → the code that already exists → the seven parts we must write → how one care cycle flows through all of them → what gets built on which day. One sentence: A Python program on the Mac that turns a teleoperated robot kit into a supervised plant caretaker that can explain every action it took. Exists · LeRobot / XLeRobot We build Deferred Human Scope One parked robot, two arms, three cameras, one light sensor, two paper trays, one bottle. Watering stays human-authorized for the whole trip. Honesty Nothing in this deck is implemented. Green boxes exist upstream; blue boxes are ours to write; grey is deferred. Navigate Arrow keys or the buttons. O opens the outline; P presents full screen. This replaces the September 22 slide set. Sources: XLeRobot repository and docs, LeRobot, the September 20 redline, purchase records. Why write anything at all · 02 / 18 The kit is a body with reflexes. The farm needs a routine, a memory and a conscience. XLeRobot gives us motors, cameras, kinematics and a way to train policies. It does not know what a tray is. What the kit does out of the box XLeRobot + LeRobot today • A person drives the arms, head and wheels with a keyboard, Xbox pad, Joy-Cons or VR. • Three cameras stream frames; joint positions read back 30× per second. • Demonstrations can be recorded to a dataset and a policy (ACT / SmolVLA / π0.5) trained on them. • An LLM-agent example turns camera + tools into “approach a human”. It has no idea what a tray, a plant, water, a schedule, a fault or “yesterday” is. The plant-watering clip in the showcase is teleoperated, sped up 8×. What a farm caretaker needs The farm program • Knows which tray it is looking at and whether the view is fresh. • Runs a fixed routine: inspect → measure → ask → pour → verify → park. • Asks a person before water moves; pours a bounded amount; returns upright. • Writes down intent, attempt and outcome before, during and after every action. • Pauses on doubt and never repeats a pour whose result is unknown. • Lets a person see why it paused and fix it from a screen. • Gets better from its own recorded episodes, in the open. the gap = this deck Exists Teleoperation, calibration, dataset recording, policy training. All Python on a laptop. Missing A schedule, tray identity, human authorization, bounded pouring, a record of what happened, pause-on-doubt, and a screen for a person. Therefore We write a farm layer on top of LeRobot and call the robot object directly. We do not fork the robot code. The showcase watering clip (0:56–0:59) is labelled “Teleoped with Switch Joycons”. No plant-care policy or checkpoint was found in the upstream repo or on the Hugging Face Hub. The physical system · 03 / 18 Everything is a USB device on one Mac Two motor boards, three cameras and one ESP32 plug into a powered hub. Motor power is separate wall supplies. MacBook Neo Runs everything. No Raspberry Pi. Python · LeRobot · our farm code RSHTECH 7-port hub Own 5 V adapter. Carries USB data only. Never powers motors. USB-C · USB 3 Motor board A → bus 1 Left arm: 6 × STS3215 servos, IDs 1–6 Head pan / tilt: IDs 7–8 USB serial on the Mac: /dev/tty.usbmodem… 12 V / 8 A wall supply (separate) Motor board B → bus 2 Right arm: 6 × STS3215 servos, IDs 1–6 Drive wheels: IDs 9–10 (disabled in V0) USB serial on the Mac: /dev/tty.usbmodem… 12 V / 8 A wall supply (separate) Three USB cameras head · left wrist · right wrist OpenCV / AVFoundation, 640×480 @ 30 fps ELEGOO ESP32 (one of three) USB serial → JSON lines to the Mac I²C: BH1750 light sensor on the paddle BH1750 light paddle Gripped tool. 4 wires: 3V3, GND, SDA (GPIO21), SCL (GPIO22). Optional SHT31 air sensor On the body, not the arm. Same I²C bus. Moisture probe + relay Deferred for paper trays. Not wired. Bottle · trays · table No electronics. Known only through cameras and taught positions. Anker C300 (in hand) + wheels Owned, not wired: wall power and parked base for the whole trip. 12 V comes from its car outlet via a fused harness, not USB-C. Two facts shape the code: Everything is a USB device on one Mac. Motion is 14 servo positions; sensing is 3 images + 1 lux number. That is the whole interface. Motion 14 servo positions (two arms + head) and, later, two wheel velocities. Motor IDs 1–8 on bus 1, 1–6 and 9–10 on bus 2 — exactly what XLerobot2Wheels expects. Sensing Three 640×480 frames per tick plus one lux number over serial. The moisture probe, air sensor, wheels and battery stay off. Passive Bottle, trays and table have no electronics. The software knows them only through taught positions and camera views. Serial port names on macOS are /dev/tty.usbmodem…, discovered with lerobot-find-port; cameras with lerobot-find-cameras. Delivered board pinouts must be read before wiring; GPIO21/22 is the proposed I²C pair for the ELEGOO ESP32. What already exists · 04 / 18 XLeRobot’s code base, layer by layer The repository is a thin extension of Hugging Face LeRobot: a robot class, an IK solver, teleop scripts and a recorder. FeetechMotorsBus Serial protocol to STS3215 servos. Read positions, load, temperature. Write goal positions. XLerobot2Wheels Two buses, 14 joints + 2 wheels. get_observation() → dict of joint.pos + camera frames send_action() → dict of joint.pos targets Calibration file per robot id. SO101Kinematics Analytical IK for the SO-101 arm. x/y/pitch → joint angles. Used by every teleop example. Teleop examples Keyboard, Xbox, Joy-Con, VR. Two-wheel keyboard script exists. This is how we teach poses. lerobot-record Records observation + action at fps into a LeRobotDataset (parquet + mp4). Optionally runs a policy. Train / run policy ACT, SmolVLA, π0.5 recipes. Needs consistent camera poses. Evaluate on the real robot. Upstream stack, bottom to top (all Python, Apache-2.0): motors → robot object → kinematics → human control → dataset → learned policy What we call directly on the Mac robot = XLerobot2Wheels(config); robot.connect() obs = robot.get_observation() # 14 joint.pos + 3 frames robot.send_action({"right_arm_wrist_flex.pos": 40.0, ...}) What we do not use in V0 ZMQ host/client: only for a Raspberry Pi on the robot. We run in-process. Wheel velocities: the base stays parked. RoboCrew LLM agent: our orchestrator owns the decision loop instead. Robot object XLerobot2Wheels opens two FeetechMotorsBus instances and the cameras. get_observation() returns joint positions and frames; send_action() takes joint targets. Calibration is a JSON file per robot id. Kinematics SO101Kinematics converts x / y / pitch to joint angles. Every teleop example uses it; our keyframe skills will too. Learning lerobot-record writes a LeRobotDataset; the ACT / SmolVLA / π0.5 guides train from it. That pipeline is ours to reuse, unchanged. Files read: software/src/robots/xlerobot_2wheels/*.py, software/src/model/SO101Robot.py, software/src/record.py, examples/4_xlerobot_2wheels_teleop_keyboard.py, docs install / teleop / VLA_ACT / LLM_agent. The ZMQ host/client exists for a Raspberry Pi and is not needed when the Mac is the controller. Architecture · 05 / 18 Eight layers, seven of them ours Commands flow down through adapters to the hardware. Observations and evidence flow up to the people and models that review them. 7 · Learning loop record episodes → train → eval vs rules → shadow → release 6 · Review exception viewer (human) · Jev (shadow) · Astra (proposals) 5 · Evidence store SQLite + images: intent → attempt → verified / UNKNOWN 4 · Care-cycle orchestrator state machine; evidence + deadline per step; pauses on doubt 3 · Perception tray id · fresh · opening visible · spill 3-state · light stats 2 · Skills go_rest · look_at · pick_tool · measure · pour · upright · place · stop 1 · Device adapters robot · cameras · ESP32 serial · human — one status vocabulary 0 · Hardware + upstream Feetech bus · XLerobot2Wheels · cameras · IK · record · train Config profile paper-tray-v0.yaml: ports, camera identities, tray positions, enabled sensors, motion limits. Simulator Fake robot, fake cameras, fake ESP32 behind the same adapter interface. Fault injection. Local safety rules Joint limits, max step per tick, servo temperature, watchdog, torque-off on disconnect. Never overridden by a model. commands ↓ observations ↑ · evidence ↑ Bottom Layer 0 is the kit and LeRobot. Layer 1 wraps every device in one status vocabulary so the rest of the program never sees a bare number. Middle Skills move; perception judges; the orchestrator sequences them with deadlines and writes evidence as it goes. Top A person reviews exceptions in a viewer. Jev and Astra observe in shadow. The learning loop turns recorded episodes into better skills and recipes. Cross-cutting One config profile names what exists. A simulator implements the adapters with fakes. Safety rules live in code and outrank everything. The next nine slides take one layer each, then trace one cycle through all of them. Layer 1 · 06 / 18 Device adapters: one interface, four devices Robot, cameras, ESP32 and the human each expose read() with a status. OK, STALE, INVALID and NOT_APPLICABLE mean different things. One interface for every device read() → {value, t, seq, status} status ∈ { OK, STALE, INVALID, NOT_APPLICABLE } — nothing upstream ever sees a bare number Robot adapter Wraps XLerobot2Wheels. joints(), frames(), move_to(targets, max_step), stop(), torque_off(). Checks load/temperature each tick. Disconnect → INVALID and a safe stop. Camera adapter Names head / left_wrist / right_wrist by device identity, never by index 0-1-2. Every frame carries capture time. Old frame → STALE. No device → INVALID. ESP32 adapter Serial JSON lines at ~5 Hz: {"seq":812,"t_ms":93410, "lux":412.5,"ok":true} Gap in seq or no line for 1 s → STALE. Sensor error flag → INVALID. Human adapter Buttons and typed confirmations from the viewer. Each one is a timestamped, signed-by-name record. Absent → the cycle waits; it does not assume. Config decides what exists enabled: robot, cameras, esp32_light disabled: sht31, moisture, wheels, pump A disabled device reads NOT_APPLICABLE forever. The orchestrator treats that differently from INVALID: “no probe” is not “dry”. Why this layer first The simulator implements the same four interfaces with fakes, so the whole program above runs on the Mac before the robot exists. Swapping fake → real is one line in the config. Robot Wraps XLerobot2Wheels. Adds per-tick load and temperature checks, a clamped move_to, and stop / torque_off. Cameras Bound by device identity, not by index — indices reshuffle on reconnect. Every frame carries its capture time. ESP32 Firmware prints one JSON line per reading with a sequence number. A gap or silence becomes STALE on the Mac side; an I²C error becomes INVALID. Human Buttons in the viewer are an input device too: each press is a named, timestamped record. NOT_APPLICABLE is the state of a device the config disabled. The orchestrator can plan around it; it can never treat it as a reading. “No probe” is not “dry”. Layer 2 · 07 / 18 Skills: eight motions with contracts Each skill states what must be true before it runs and what is true after. The orchestrator only ever calls skills, never joints. Skill Needs before True after Arm go_rest() any arms at rest pose, grippers as-is both look_at(tray) tray known head + wrist cameras framed on tray head pick_tool(paddle | bottle) gripper empty, tool in rest tool gripped; grip verified by gripper position one arm measure_pose(tray) paddle gripped paddle level at canopy height, arm out of light left pour(tray, tilt°, s) bottle gripped, fill known, human OK tilt held for s seconds, then upright right return_upright() bottle gripped bottle vertical; commanded before any release right place_tool() tool gripped, rest free tool in rest, gripper open, arm clear one arm stop() any motion halted; torque held or off per rule both v1 · taught keyframes (Sep 30 – Oct 5) Drive the arm with the keyboard teleop, save joint positions as named keyframes, interpolate with the IK and a max-step clamp. Every skill is a short list of keyframes plus checks. Boring, inspectable, fixable. v2 · learned policies (after ~50 demos) Record pick_tool / pour with lerobot-record, train ACT, run it behind the same skill interface. Only replaces a v1 skill after it wins on held-out episodes. Camera poses must match recording. v1 Keyframes taught with the upstream keyboard teleop, interpolated with the IK solver and the max-step clamp. Readable, editable, no training. Contracts pour() refuses to run without a gripped bottle, a known fill and a human authorization record. return_upright() is always commanded before any release. v2 A skill may later be replaced by an ACT policy trained on our own demonstrations, behind the same interface, after it wins on held-out episodes. Pour parameters are tilt angle and seconds, calibrated into a kitchen measuring cup across fill levels. A tilt duration is never recorded as millilitres. Layer 3 · 08 / 18 Perception: six outputs, each with an unknown From three frames, joint positions and the lux stream, perception answers a fixed set of questions with typed values. Inputs 3 frames + capture time current joint positions ESP32 lux stream tray_id which tray, from its fixed nest position (+ optional AprilTag) ↳ UNKNOWN if the nest is empty or the view is off fresh frame age < 1 s and camera matches its name ↳ STALE otherwise; nothing downstream runs on stale opening_visible refill opening clear and reachable in the wrist view ↳ UNKNOWN if occluded or dark spill CLEAR / SPILL / UNKNOWN around the tray after a pour ↳ an unseen area can never be CLEAR growth green-pixel fraction from the same head pose each day ↳ a trend for people, not a decision input light median lux, spread, saturation over ~10 fresh conversions ↳ INVALID if arm shadow or sensor error The one rule Every output has an UNKNOWN value and the cycle treats UNKNOWN as “stop and ask”, never as “fine”. v1 → v2 v1: OpenCV colour / tag / difference checks. v2: a vision model on the same frames. Same typed outputs. Identity Trays live in fixed nests, so tray_id comes from position; AprilTags are an optional upgrade for trays that move. Freshness A frame older than one second, or from a camera that is not the one its name claims, blocks the cycle. Spill Three values. An area the camera cannot see is UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN after a pour pauses the cycle for a human look. Growth and light Green fraction and lux statistics are for people and for cohort comparison. They never decide a pour. v1 is OpenCV: nest occupancy, colour and frame differencing. v2 may be a vision model, but it must return the same typed outputs. Camera spill detection is experimental and gets its own fault tests. Layer 4 · 09 / 18 The care cycle: a state machine that would rather stop than guess Eleven states, one human gate, two ways to pause. Every arrow requires named evidence and has a deadline. IDLE IDENTIFY INSPECT MEASURE LIGHT ASK HUMAN PICK BOTTLE APPROACH POUR RETURN UPRIGHT VERIFY PARK evidence + deadline on every arrow no “yes” → PARK, no water PAUSED (reason, evidence) Any check fails, any deadline passes, any adapter goes INVALID or STALE. Motors stop; bottle is returned upright first if it is held. UNKNOWN DELIVERY Crash or lost acknowledgement between POUR and VERIFY. Stays UNKNOWN until a person reconciles. Automatic retry is not an option. Human review Re-inspect, confirm physically, authorize, resolve, or take over. Only a person leaves PAUSED. Timeouts: identify 10 s · inspect 20 s · measure 15 s · ask 10 min · pick 30 s · pour ≤ 4 s tilt · verify 20 s · park 30 s (starting values, all in the config). Happy path identify → inspect → measure light → ask human → pick bottle → approach → pour → return upright → verify → park. The gate ASK_HUMAN shows the evidence in the viewer and waits. No answer within the deadline means park, not pour. Pause Any failed check or timed-out step enters PAUSED with its reason and evidence. Only a person leaves it. Unknown A crash between the tilt and the verify leaves the pour UNKNOWN. The cycle will not retry; a person reconciles. Deadlines are starting values in the config. Pick / dock / weigh states from the redline belong to a future pod-moving profile and are not in this machine. Layer 5 · 10 / 18 Evidence store: intent, attempt, outcome — in that order SQLite for metadata, files for images, append-only everywhere. “We sent the command” and “water reached the tray” are separate rows. cycles cycle_id, tray_id, profile, code_version, config_hash, calibration_id, simulated, started, ended, result observations obs_id, cycle_id, source, t, status, value_json, image_hash, extractor_version decisions decision_id, cycle_id, kind (rule | human | jev_shadow), inputs_ref, choice, probabilities, schema_version actions action_id, cycle_id, skill, params, INTENT_t, ATTEMPT_t, RESULT ∈ {VERIFIED, ABORTED, UNKNOWN}, VERIFY_t, evidence_ref interventions who, t, what was physically checked, what was done, minutes spent One pour, written three times INTENT written before any motor command ATTEMPT written before the tilt can move water VERIFY written after the wrist camera confirms crash here → RESULT = UNKNOWN Rules Append-only. Images stored by content hash, never overwritten. Duplicate action_id returns the existing record — the database cannot make a pour happen exactly once, only refuse to pretend. Nightly backup with a restore test. What the store never contains A number without a status and a time. An estimated volume labelled as measured. “Delivered” inferred from “the servo finished moving”. Secrets, network credentials or addresses. Five tables cycles, observations, decisions, actions, interventions. Every row carries code version, config hash and calibration id. Three writes per pour INTENT before any motor command, ATTEMPT before the tilt can move water, VERIFY after the camera confirms. A crash in between reads as UNKNOWN forever. Never A value without a status and time; an estimate labelled as measured; “delivered” inferred from “servo finished”; any secret. Idempotent action ids stop a restart from double-recording; they cannot stop physics from double-pouring. That is why UNKNOWN blocks retries. Nightly backup includes a restore test. Layer 6a · 11 / 18 The exception viewer: the reason, the evidence and the eligible next steps A local web page on the Mac. When the robot pauses it shows the latest frame, its age, the reason and only the actions that are safe. localhost:8765 · farm viewer · tray B · cycle 0042 latest wrist frame age 0.6 s · right_wrist PAUSED reason: spill = UNKNOWN after pour (area under the rim not visible from right_wrist) last verified: RETURN_UPRIGHT ✓ 12:04:31 · fill ~40 mL (human, 11:58) evidence: obs 9124 · action 771 · decision rule:spill_gate Eligible next steps Re-inspect from head camera I looked: no spill, paper wet I looked: spill — cleaned, resolved Caretaker takes over this tray Retry pour — not offered while delivery is UNKNOWN Every press → intervention record: who, when, what was checked. Shadow (later): Jev suggested inspect_water 0.71 — logged, not acted on. Local network only. Not a safety device — stop rules live in the controller. Shows Current state, last verified action, why it paused, which observation and rule produced the pause. Offers Re-inspect, confirm a physical check, authorize one pour, mark resolved, hand the tray to a caretaker. Each press becomes an intervention record. Never offers Retry pour while delivery is UNKNOWN. The button does not exist in that state. Reachable from a phone on the same Wi-Fi; not exposed to the internet. Not a safety device — the stop rules run in the controller whether or not anyone is looking. Layer 6b · 12 / 18 Jev and Astra: advice with no hands Rules own protection. Jev classifies evidence into typed choices. Astra investigates exceptions and proposes changes. Neither can move a servo. Evidence packet tray_id, age, recent pours, sensor statuses, image features, device faults, last action, allowed next steps. Small, typed, timestamped. Local rules (must pass) Numeric bounds, freshness, device health, human authorization present. Own machine protection. Run without any network. Gate → one preapproved skill Only a skill from the allowed list can execute, and only if rules passed. A model label is never permission to move or pour. Jev · typed classifier (shadow) Q1 evidence quality → usable | reacquire | conflicting | unknown Q2 next review → routine | inspect_water | inspect_image | review_machine | review_hygiene | unknown Returns choice + probabilities. Abstains on unknown. suggestion only, logged Astra · reasoner (offline) Reads exception packets and daily summaries. Proposes one specific change with evidence, expected benefit and a rollback condition. Never writes servo commands. Never on the protection path. Human caretaker Physical checks, authorizations, ambiguous crop calls, final incident labels. The only party that leaves PAUSED. Earning a role: shadow → compare → limited pilot Replay the same recorded episodes through rules-only, rules+Jev, rules+Astra. Report recall per fault class, false clearances, abstention rate, review minutes, p95 latency, cost. Target ≥120 labelled episodes, ≥10 per priority fault (stale sensor, missing tray, obscured view, failed pour, camera loss). Jev gets an operational role only if it beats rules-only on a held-out set — and even then only to route reviews, not to pour. Jev Two narrow questions per packet — evidence quality and next review — with probabilities and an explicit unknown. Runs in shadow: logged next to the rule’s decision, compared later. Astra Reads exception packets and daily summaries offline. One proposal at a time, with evidence, expected benefit and a rollback condition. Earning a role Shadow → replay comparison on ≥120 labelled episodes → limited pilot. Even then Jev only routes reviews. The existing Goose/Jev helper routes documents with a 0.85 threshold; a farm adapter must add explicit farm questions, abstention labels and preserved confidence metadata. Cloud calls stay off the protection path. Layer 7 · 13 / 18 The learning loop: skills graduate, recipes change between cohorts Robot learning reuses LeRobot’s recorder and trainers on our own episodes. Crop learning is A/B cohorts with one difference at a time. Teleop keyboard / Joy-Con drive of one arm; farm cameras fixed lerobot-record ≈50 episodes per skill: pick_tool, pour into cup LeRobotDataset parquet + mp4, our tray, our bottle, our poses Train ACT on the Mac or a rented GPU; version the checkpoint Offline replay candidate vs v1 keyframe skill on held-out episodes Shadow policy proposes, keyframes execute; log disagreement Limited pilot empty bottle, then cup, then tray; rollback ready Robot learning: a skill graduates from v1 to v2 Crop learning: recipes change between frozen cohorts, never inside one Cohort A · Sep 30 Cress on paper, recipe A. Every pour, light reading and human minute recorded. Cohort B · Oct 3 Same seed lot, one deliberate difference (e.g. light position). Same records. Proposal C Astra summarises A vs B and proposes one change with a rollback condition. A person accepts or not. What is honest to say today No pretrained watering policy exists anywhere we looked; the two “water” datasets on the Hub are bottle transport. The upstream demo is teleoperated. Training happens on our own episodes or not at all, and logging alone improves nothing. Robot Teleop ≈50 demonstrations per skill → LeRobotDataset → ACT → offline replay against the keyframe skill → shadow → limited pilot with rollback. Crop Cohort A on Sep 30, B on Oct 3 from the same seed lot. Astra proposes C from their records; a person decides. Discipline Simulated and real episodes are never mixed. Nothing is tuned on the evaluation set. A recipe never changes mid-cohort except as a recorded deviation. No pretrained watering policy exists; both “water” datasets on the Hub are bottle transport. Training is optional inside the trip (see decisions). End to end · 14 / 18 One cycle, thirteen messages, seven lanes Follow a single authorized pour from the first camera frame to the shadow classification. Hardware Adapters Perception Orchestrator Evidence Human Jev (shadow) 1. read joints, 3 frames, lux 2. observations with status 3. tray B · fresh · opening visible · light 410 lx 4. decision: rules pass → ASK_HUMAN 5. viewer: “tray B looks dry at edge — authorize 1 pour?” 6. authorize (name, time) → intervention record 7. action INTENT pour(B, 35°, 2 s) 8. skill pick_bottle → approach → pour 9. send_action(joint targets, clamped) 10. ATTEMPT written before tilt 11. spill CLEAR · opening wet → VERIFIED 12. RESULT VERIFIED · PARK 13. packet → “routine” 0.88 (logged only) 1–4 Adapters read; perception judges tray B fresh and reachable; rules pass; the orchestrator decides to ask. 5–6 The viewer shows the edge-of-paper frame; a person authorizes one pour; the record names them. 7–10 INTENT, then skills, then clamped joint targets, then ATTEMPT — written before the tilt. 11–13 Perception verifies wetness and no spill; result VERIFIED; the packet goes to Jev in shadow. Replace step 11 with “spill UNKNOWN” and the cycle enters PAUSED; replace a crash between 10 and 11 and the action stays UNKNOWN. Both paths are on the state-machine slide. Building it before the robot exists · 15 / 18 The simulator is the same program with fakes plugged in Because everything above layer 1 talks to adapters, fakes make the whole farm program runnable on the Mac this week. Farm program (unchanged) orchestrator perception evidence store viewer skills Adapter interface read() → status move_to() frames() lux() confirm() Real devices XLerobot2Wheels OpenCV cameras ESP32 serial browser buttons Fakes FakeRobot: kinematic model, instant or slow FakeCamera: replays saved frames FakeESP32: scripted lux FakeHuman: scripted answers Fault injection stale frame camera unplugged serial gap servo overtemp crash after ATTEMPT human never answers wrong tray in nest lost acknowledgement Every simulated record carries simulated = true, so fake episodes can never be counted as farm evidence. This is what gets built first, on the Mac, before the robot exists — and it stays as the regression suite forever. Fakes FakeRobot with a kinematic model, FakeCamera replaying saved frames, FakeESP32 with scripted lux, FakeHuman with scripted answers. Faults Stale frames, unplugged camera, serial gaps, overtemp, crash after ATTEMPT, silent human, wrong tray. Each has a test. Forever The fakes become the regression suite. Every later change to the orchestrator runs against them first. All simulated records carry simulated = true. They are never counted as farm evidence or used to tune thresholds for the real system. Config, safety, deferrals · 16 / 18 One profile names what exists; code enforces what may move The config profile lists ports, camera identities, tray nests and enabled sensors. Safety limits are code and outrank every model. profile: paper-tray-v0 robot: port1: /dev/tty.usbmodem58A6… port2: /dev/tty.usbmodem58B1… max_relative_target: 8 wheels: disabled cameras: head: {id: "USB Camera 0C45:6366-1"} right_wrist: {id: "…-2"} sensors: {esp32_light: on, sht31: off, moisture: off} trays: B: {nest: right_front, pour_pose: kf_pour_B_v3} limits: {tilt_max: 40, pour_s_max: 4, temp_max: 55} Local safety rules (code, not config) Joint range from calibration; refuse targets outside it. Max step per tick — the arm cannot jump. Servo temperature / load ceiling → stop. Watchdog: no fresh observation for 0.5 s → stop. Disconnect → torque off (upstream default), after return_upright if a bottle is held. No model output can relax any of these. See the planter renders Inspect, rinse and leak-test Remove loose plastic, rinse with cool water and check the fit without forcing clips. Put the empty trough/outer tray on dry kitchen paper inside an existing dish. Add a modest amount of water below the growing surface. Inspect after 30 minutes and again later that day. Any wet patch underneath fails the test: use another dish for growing while repairing/reprinting. The 30-minute check is our proposed initial screen, not a leak certification. Days 1–2 · check the water path Morning and evening: check the trough, paper at several spots, and the dry surface underneath. Add only enough water to keep paper evenly damp. Photograph from the same angle. Some seed may swell or begin rooting; slower emergence is still possible. Days 2–4 · look for emergence When shoots establish, uncover and give bright light. Log first roots, upright shoots and seed leaves. If a patch is dry while the trough has water, fix wick contact instead of adding more water blindly. Day 6 · record and review Take final photos, compare the two kits, list changes and export the notebook. Decide whether to continue the crop or end it and clean/dry the prints. Keep the paper damp, not submerged. Avoid blasting seeds with a direct pour. The shoots are pale or leaning Uncover after emergence and improve light without overheating. Use the same camera angle to track changes; brightness in a phone photo alone is not a light-meter reading. Nothing has emerged by day 4 Check seed identity/packet guidance, freshness, paper moisture and temperature. Compare the household reference if you started one. Don’t keep increasing water; saturated seeds can also fail. Slime, fuzzy growth or an unpleasant smell Cress produces clear gel around wet seeds. Root hairs can look fuzzy, while spreading fuzzy patches, discoloration or a bad smell warrant stopping and discarding the affected trial. A photo alone may not distinguish them reliably. A clean kitchen tray/dish underneath, a small cup or spoon, and a phone camera. A household loose cover if the cress planter needs humidity retention; square kit includes its cover. No growing soil, fertilizer, purchased mats, sensors or robot needed for this short paper trial. What “self-watering” means The rectangular planter stores a little water below the seeds. Paper carries it upward by capillary action. You still check it and refill by hand. The square kit has a cover and removable insert, but it does not automatically wick unless its growing medium makes the needed connection to water. See the planter renders Inspect, rinse and leak-test Remove loose plastic, rinse with cool water and check the fit without forcing clips. Put the empty trough/outer tray on dry kitchen paper inside an existing dish. Add a modest amount of water below the growing surface. Inspect after 30 minutes and again later that day. Any wet patch underneath fails the test: use another dish for growing while repairing/reprinting. The 30-minute check is our proposed initial screen, not a leak certification. PLA prints may retain residue and are not established food-contact equipment. Treat unknown-filament prints as growth/mechanical tests; use a suitable food-growing container for any batch intended to eat. Avoid boiling water or a hot dishwasher on the PLA parts. Make the wick actually touch the water For the rectangular planter: snap its four insets into the holder. Feed paper down into each inset and lay 3–4 layers across the seed platform, maintaining a continuous wet-paper path. Pre-wet the paper, drain surface puddles and fill the trough below the seed platform. The creator suggests about 80% full; don’t use that as an excuse to submerge seeds. For the square kit: put damp paper on the perforated insert inside its outer tray. Keep it moist from above initially; only rely on bottom water after confirming paper/root contact or a working wick. Water underneath an air gap cannot wet the paper automatically. Sow a small, even patch Scatter dry cress seeds onto moist paper, with no thick piles. Do not pre-soak cress: it becomes sticky when wet. One packet is enough for small test patches; there is no need to densely fill the entire large tray. Give both kits similar seeded patch areas and density, using the same seed lot. Keep an unseeded edge on the same sheet for moisture checks. Use a phone note or tape already at home to label A = wick planter, B = square tray, and optionally C = household dish. A household reference can help distinguish seed trouble from a printed-container problem; it is not a controlled scientific experiment. Keep the first stage damp, then give it light Follow the seed packet’s conditions. A loose cover can reduce early drying; check at least morning and evening and do not seal it airtight. Remove the cover when shoots emerge and begin standing up; use the plant’s condition rather than an automatic date. Then place it in bright natural light away from intense window heat, radiators and cold drafts. An ordinary comfortable room is a practical starting point. Leave airflow around the seedlings. Never leave a covered tray baking in direct sun. Assembly steps adapted from Macce’s planter instructions ; cress sowing/early growth from Seedmart . Our leak screens, comparisons and log schedule are proposed tests. The tray setup is an adaptation to the actual printed kit, not a claim that the seed supplier tested these prints.

title: The first six days of any trial
text: Illustrative observations, not a promised timetable. Log what your crop actually does. Open the image for a larger view. The first six days of any trial Day 0 · fit, water and sow Complete the leak/wick checks, photograph the dry assembly and first sowing. Record crop, date, paper layers, seeded area and starting water level. Measure water with kitchen utensils only if practical; otherwise record “not measured”. Days 1–2 · check the water path Morning and evening: check the trough, paper at several spots, and the dry surface underneath. Add only enough water to keep paper evenly damp. Photograph from the same angle. Some seed may swell or begin rooting; slower emergence is still possible. Days 2–4 · look for emergence When shoots establish, uncover and give bright light. Log first roots, upright shoots and seed leaves. If a patch is dry while the trough has water, fix wick contact instead of adding more water blindly. Days 4–5 · test useful repeatability Compare wetness across the tray, count manual top-ups and note any leak or wilt. Practice tiny hand pours at the refill opening using your kitchen measure. Do not deliberately drought-stress the live crop; test dry/damp/wet sensor samples separately if electronics are available. Day 6 · record and review Take final photos, compare the two kits, list changes and export the notebook. Decide whether to continue the crop or end it and clean/dry the prints. What a first trial can prove: visible germination, a reliable water path, no observed leaks, a known manual refill routine and photos/notes explaining failures. This does not establish autonomous care, edible-product safety or a guaranteed number of unattended days.

title: What a problem looks like
text: What a problem looks like There is water below, but the paper is dry The paper may not reach the reservoir, the wick may have separated, or the tray may be tilted. Re-wet and reconnect it. Check multiple points. Don’t drown the seeds to compensate for an air gap. Seeds are floating or the surface is puddled Remove excess water gently and lower the water level. Keep the paper damp, not submerged. Avoid blasting seeds with a direct pour. The shoots are pale or leaning Uncover after emergence and improve light without overheating. Use the same camera angle to track changes; brightness in a phone photo alone is not a light-meter reading. Nothing has emerged by day 4 Check seed identity/packet guidance, freshness, paper moisture and temperature. Compare the household reference if you started one. Don’t keep increasing water; saturated seeds can also fail. Slime, fuzzy growth or an unpleasant smell Cress produces clear gel around wet seeds. Root hairs can look fuzzy, while spreading fuzzy patches, discoloration or a bad smell warrant stopping and discarding the affected trial. A photo alone may not distinguish them reliably. Don’t eat an uncertain batch; clean the container before restarting.
